Arsenic sulphide sol, As₂S₃, is a **negatively** charged sol, so it is coagulated by the positive
ion of the added electrolyte.
The flocculation value is the minimum concentration needed to coagulate, so the **minimum**
flocculation value belongs to the **most effective** cation.
By the Hardy–Schulze rule, coagulating power rises steeply with the charge on that ion —
roughly as the sixth power of the charge:
Al³⁺ > Ca²⁺ ≈ Mg²⁺ > Na⁺
Al³⁺ carries the highest charge, neutralises the negative particles most efficiently, and so needs
the smallest concentration.
In figures, the flocculation value for As₂S₃ is about 55 mmol L⁻¹ for NaCl but only 0.09 for
AlCl₃ — a difference of several hundred times.
∴ Al³⁺.
kcet|Chemistry|2013|58||0|0:
The second law of thermodynamics says the entropy of an **isolated** system can only increase
or stay the same for a reversible change; for any real, spontaneous process it increases.
The solar system is effectively isolated — energy radiates away but it exchanges nothing with
any surroundings that could lower its entropy.
Everything happening inside it is irreversible: nuclear fusion in the sun, radiation spreading
out into space, friction, mixing. Each of those processes generates entropy.
So the total entropy of the solar system rises continuously.
It cannot be constant (3), because that would require every process to be reversible, and it
cannot decrease (2) without violating the second law.
This is the direction that defines the arrow of time.
∴ increasing.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|1||0|0.s:
By Raoult's law the relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the mole fraction of the solute.
A 20% lowering means:
χsolute = 0.20
Moles of octane, C₈H₁₈, molar mass 114:
n(octane) = 114 / 114 = 1 mol
Let n be the moles of solute:
n / (n + 1) = 0.20
n = 0.20n + 0.20
0.80n = 0.20
n = 0.25 mol
mass = moles × molar mass = 0.25 × 40 = 10 g
Note the solvent moles must stay in the denominator. Using n/1 = 0.2 would give 0.2 mol and
8 g, which is the common error — acceptable only for very dilute solutions, and 20% is not dilute.
∴ 10 g.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|2||0|0:
Think about what happens physically when a gas sticks to a solid surface.
ΔS < 0 — the gas molecules lose their freedom to roam in three dimensions and become confined
to a two-dimensional surface. Disorder falls, so entropy decreases.
ΔG < 0 — adsorption happens spontaneously, so the free energy change must be negative.
ΔH < 0 — now use ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Since ΔS is negative, the term −TΔS is **positive**. For ΔG
to come out negative despite that, ΔH must be negative and large enough to overcome it.
So adsorption is necessarily **exothermic**, and that conclusion is forced by the other two signs
rather than assumed.
It also explains why physisorption decreases as temperature rises: the +(−TΔS) term grows
with T until ΔG turns positive and the gas desorbs.
∴ ΔG < 0, ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|5||0|0.s:
At equilibrium the cell potential is related to the equilibrium constant by the Nernst equation:
E°cell = (2.303RT/nF)·log K
The bracket in the question tells us 2.303RT/F = 0.059, so
E°cell = (0.059/n)·log K
Find n from the equation A(s) + 2B⁺ ⇌ A²⁺ + 2B(s): A goes from 0 to +2, so two electrons are
transferred, n = 2.
Substitute:
0.0295 = (0.059/2)·log K
0.0295 = 0.0295 × log K
log K = 1
K = 10¹ = 10
The numbers are chosen so that E°cell is exactly half of 0.059, making log K come out at 1.
∴ K = 10.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|6||0|0:
Find the molecular formula first, then identify the compound, then its functional isomer.
Percentages: C 52%, H 13%, so oxygen makes up 100 − 52 − 13 = 35%.
Relative moles:
C : 52/12 = 4.33
H : 13/1 = 13
O : 35/16 = 2.19
Divide by the smallest, 2.19: C = 2, H = 6, O = 1 ⇒ empirical formula C₂H₆O.
Molar mass = 2 × vapour density = 2 × 23 = 46, and C₂H₆O already weighs 46, so the molecular
formula is C₂H₆O too.
It reacts with sodium liberating hydrogen, which means a free –OH group, so the compound is
**ethanol**, C₂H₅OH. (An ether would not react with sodium.)
A functional isomer has the same formula but a different functional group: C₂H₆O as an ether
is CH₃–O–CH₃, methoxymethane.
∴ methoxy methane.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|7||0|0.s:
Find the statement that is not true.
(2) True — the electromeric effect lasts only while the attacking reagent is present and
disappears the moment it is removed. It is temporary.
(3) True — it requires a multiple bond, since it is the π electrons that shift.
(4) True — it is not spontaneous; it is called into being by an approaching reagent.
(1) False — the charges produced are **full**, not partial. In the electromeric effect the shared
pair is transferred **completely** to one of the two atoms:
>C=C< + reagent ⇒ >C⁺–C⁻<
That gives one carbon a whole positive charge and the other a whole negative charge.
Partial charges, written δ+ and δ−, belong to the **inductive** effect, where σ electrons are only
slightly displaced along a chain. Confusing the two is exactly what this question tests.
∴ statement (1) is not true.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|8||0|0:
Sodium in dry ether couples the two carbons that carry halogens. With a **mixture** of two
different halides, all three possible pairings occur — this is the Wurtz–Fittig reaction.
The halides are CH₃Br and C₆H₅Br, so the couplings are:
CH₃ + CH₃ ⇒ CH₃–CH₃, ethane ✓
C₆H₅ + C₆H₅ ⇒ C₆H₅–C₆H₅, diphenyl (biphenyl) ✓
CH₃ + C₆H₅ ⇒ C₆H₅–CH₃, toluene ✓ — the cross-coupled product the reaction is used for
Every product is built from a C1 and a C6 fragment, so only C2, C7 and C12 skeletons are
possible.
Propane needs three carbons in a row, which would require joining a methyl to an ethyl — and
no ethyl fragment exists here.
∴ propane is not formed.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|9||0|0.s:
Power alcohol is a motor fuel in which ethanol replaces part of the petrol.
Its composition is about **80% petrol with 20% ethanol**, together with a small quantity of
benzene.
The benzene is not fuel in its own right here; it is added as a co-solvent. Petrol is a
hydrocarbon and ethanol is polar, so the two separate when traces of water are present.
Benzene blends with both and keeps the mixture homogeneous.
The advantages are that ethanol can be made by fermentation, so it is renewable, and that it
raises the octane rating and reduces carbon monoxide in the exhaust.
Options (3) and (4) have far too much ethanol, and (1) wrongly swaps the roles of benzene and
ethanol.
∴ 80% petrol + 20% ethanol + a small quantity of benzene.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|10||0|0:
This is the cumene process, the industrial route to phenol.
Step 1 — benzene with 2-chloropropane and anhydrous AlCl₃: Friedel–Crafts alkylation, losing HCl:
A = C₆H₅–CH(CH₃)₂, isopropylbenzene, better known as **cumene**.
Step 2 — cumene with O₂ at 130 °C: air oxidises the benzylic C–H, which is the weakest bond in
the molecule because the resulting radical is tertiary and benzylic:
B = C₆H₅–C(CH₃)₂–O–O–H, cumene hydroperoxide.
Step 3 — dilute H₂SO₄ at 100 °C: the hydroperoxide rearranges and then hydrolyses, splitting
into two useful products:
C₆H₅C(CH₃)₂OOH ⇒ C₆H₅OH + CH₃COCH₃
So alongside the phenol, C is propanone (acetone).
The process is used industrially precisely because both products are valuable; the acetone is
not a waste by-product.
∴ C is propanone.
